13.新宿区: From Naitō-Shinjuku, a new post town opened on the Kōshū road in 1698 on land of the Naitō lords of Takatō.
13.江東区: "East of the river" — east of the Sumida; chosen over Tatsumi, Higashi and Eitai.
13.大田区: One character each from Ōmori and Kamata, the two wards merged in 1947.
13.杉並区: From the row of cedars planted along the Ōme road by the lord of Narimune and Tabata villages in the early Edo period.
13.板橋区: From the "plank bridge" carrying the old Nakasendō over the Shakujii River.
13.練馬区: Several theories: Nerima Castle; a "neriba" where red loam was kneaded; or the Nara-period post station Norinuma.
13.足立区: From Adachi district of Musashi, set up after the Taika reforms.
13.葛飾区: Katsushika was the name of a wide district of Shimōsa, already in the Man'yōshū; this area itself was called Kasai until early modern times.
13.江戸川区: From the Edo River on its eastern edge; "Matsue-ku", after the planned ward office, was considered first.
13.八王子市: From the Hachiōji shrine and Hachiōji Castle named after it.
13.町田市: Theories: "machi" as a block of paddy; a busy market (machi = ichi); or "matsurida", fields kept for the market god.
13.北区: When Ōji and Takinogawa wards merged, the candidates included Jōhoku, Asukayama and Akabane. Asukayama was the favourite but thought hard to read, so the plain compass name Kita ("north") won.
13.豊島区: When four towns of Kita-Toshima District joined Tokyo City they took the district name, which goes back to ancient Toshima District in Musashi. The city first proposed Ikebukuro, then Mejiro, before petitions settled on Toshima.
13.墨田区: Takes "sumi" (墨) from Bokutei, the popular name of the Sumida riverbank, and "da" from the Sumida River. Most people wanted 隅田, but 隅 was not on the official list of characters for general use.
13.府中市: Fuchū means "seat of the provincial government": the capital of ancient Musashi Province stood here.
13.港区: The shortlist narrowed to Jōnan and Higashi-minato ("east port", for the Port of Tokyo). "Tōkyō-to Higashi-minato-ku" repeated sounds, so the "east" was dropped, leaving Minato.
13.調布市: Under the ancient tax system the "chō" levy was paid in local produce — here, cloth (fu).
13.文京区: An auspicious coinage from the merger of Koishikawa and Hongō wards: short, easy to write, and fitting the area's image as a centre of learning (bunkyō). Keihoku, Kasuga and Yushima were also proposed.
13.荒川区: Named after the Arakawa River. Since 1965, when the Arakawa Drainage Channel became the official main stream, the river through the ward has been the Sumida — but the name stayed. Tokyo City had first proposed Mikawashima, the planned site of the ward office.
13.台東区: Shitaya and Asakusa could not agree (Ueno versus Higashi). The governor proposed "Taitō", already used by a Shitaya primary school: "tai" for the Ueno heights and "tō" for the old town to their east.
13.西東京市: When Tanashi and Hōya merged, a public call produced five finalists — Nishi-Tōkyō, Keyakino, Kita-Tama, Hibari and Midorino — and a residents' survey picked Nishi-Tōkyō.
13.小平市: Coined at the 1889 merger of seven villages: "ko" from Ogawa, the main village, and "taira" for the flat land of the Musashino plateau.
13.日野市: Uncertain. One Edo gazetteer says the provincial capital's signal-fire post stood here ("tobuhino", fire field); another records the Nishi band's founder Himatsuri Muneyori enshrining a Hino deity.
13.立川市: Two theories: seen from the provincial capital, the Tama River ran "upright" (tate) past the east–west Tama hills, giving "tate no kawa"; or the local Tachikawa clan built a fort at today's Fusai-ji.
13.中央区: At the geographic centre of old Tokyo City and its business heart — the first place in Japan officially named "Chūō" (central). Edo, Ginza and Ōedo were also proposed.
13.東村山市: The eastern end of Murayama in Musashi — home of the Murayama warrior band, at the southern foot of the Sayama hills, which were called "mureyama" (massed hills).
